test_catalog.name: Pure Tone Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Pure-Tone Audiometry (PTA) is a behavioural test used to determine hearing thresholds at different frequencies using pure tones, helping to identify the degree, type, and configuration of hearing loss. (Age range: 5 years and above.)
test_catalog.preparation: Nothing special is needed. If you have a cold, a blocked ear or an ear infection on the day, tell the audiologist — it can affect the result and may be worth rescheduling.

test_catalog.name: Speech Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Assesses ability to hear and understand spoken words.

test_catalog.name: Tympanometry
test_catalog.description: Evaluates middle-ear function and eardrum mobility.

test_catalog.name: Otoacoustic Emissions
test_catalog.description: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) are low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of the cochlea in response to sound stimulation. They are recorded in the ear canal to evaluate cochlear function and are commonly used for newborn hearing screening and the assessment of cochlear integrity. (Age range: applicable for all ages.)
test_catalog.preparation: For babies: feed the baby just before the appointment — a settled, sleeping baby gives the best result. The room must be quiet, and the test cannot be completed if the baby is crying.

test_catalog.name: Speech in Noise Test
test_catalog.description: Measures how well you follow speech when there is background noise. Many people hear well in a quiet room but struggle in a crowd, and this test captures that specific difficulty.
test_catalog.preparation: No preparation needed.

test_catalog.name: Tinnitus Assessment
test_catalog.description: Characterises tinnitus pitch, loudness, and impact.

test_catalog.name: Loudness Discomfort Level
test_catalog.description: Finds the level at which sound becomes uncomfortably loud for you. This sets the safe upper limit when a hearing aid is programmed, so it never becomes painful.
test_catalog.preparation: You are in control throughout and can stop at any point. Tell the audiologist as soon as a sound is uncomfortable — you are not expected to tolerate it.

test_catalog.name: Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potential
test_catalog.description: Evaluates otolith and vestibular pathway function.

test_catalog.name: Videonystagmography
test_catalog.description: Assesses the balance organs of the inner ear by recording eye movements with goggles while you follow lights and change position. Brief dizziness during the test is expected and settles quickly.
test_catalog.preparation: Important: avoid alcohol for 48 hours and, unless your doctor says otherwise, stop anti-dizziness or sedative medication for 48 hours — these suppress the responses being measured. Eat only a light meal, wear no eye make-up, and bring someone to accompany you home.

test_catalog.name: Posturography
test_catalog.description: Measures postural stability and balance control.

test_catalog.name: Ear Evaluation (ENT)
test_catalog.description: Clinical ear examination by an ENT specialist.

test_catalog.name: Immittance Test
test_catalog.description: Battery of middle-ear tests including tympanometry and reflexes.

test_catalog.name: Auditory Brainstem Response
test_catalog.description: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) is an electrophysiologic test that measures the electrical activity generated by the auditory nerve and brainstem in response to acoustic stimuli, using surface electrodes placed on the scalp. (Age range: applicable for all ages.)
test_catalog.preparation: The patient must be asleep or lying completely still. For infants, keep the baby awake beforehand and bring a feed so they settle at the clinic; wash the hair and use no oil or cream, as the stickers must grip the skin. Allow up to two hours in total. For older children, sedation is sometimes arranged in advance — the department will tell you if fasting is required.

test_catalog.name: Middle Latency Response
test_catalog.description: Evaluates middle-latency auditory evoked potentials.

test_catalog.name: Late Latency Response
test_catalog.description: Assesses cortical auditory processing.

test_catalog.name: Cognitive Evoked Potential (P300)
test_catalog.description: Detects attention and cognitive hearing processing.

test_catalog.name: P500 Response
test_catalog.description: Evaluates higher-level auditory discrimination.

test_catalog.name: Speech Reception Threshold
test_catalog.description: Lowest level at which speech is understood.

test_catalog.name: Word Recognition Score
test_catalog.description: Tests clarity of word recognition at conversational levels.

test_catalog.name: Phonetically Balanced Tests
test_catalog.description: Measures speech discrimination with phonetically balanced words.

test_catalog.name: Visual Reinforcement Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Visual Reinforcement Audiometry (VRA) is a behavioural hearing assessment procedure in which a child’s head-turn response to an auditory stimulus is conditioned and reinforced with a visual reward (e.g., an illuminated or animated toy) to estimate hearing thresholds. (Age range: 6 months–2 years.)
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the child when they are usually alert and content, not near nap or feed time. A parent stays in the room throughout. Bring a favourite quiet toy, and avoid noisy toys or phones during the test.

test_catalog.name: Behavioural Observation Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Observes infant responses to sound in a controlled setting.

test_catalog.name: Auditory Steady State Response
test_catalog.description: An electrical test related to ABR that estimates hearing thresholds at each pitch. It is often used alongside ABR to plan a hearing aid for a baby.
test_catalog.preparation: The same preparation as ABR: the patient must be asleep or perfectly still, with clean hair and no oil. Usually done in the same session as ABR.

test_catalog.name: Play Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Play-based hearing test suited for preschool children.

test_catalog.name: Speech Detection Threshold
test_catalog.description: Lowest level at which speech is detected (not necessarily understood).

test_catalog.name: High Frequency Audiometry
test_catalog.description: An extension of the standard hearing test into very high pitches, above the usual range. Damage from loud noise or certain medicines often shows up here first, before ordinary hearing is affected.
test_catalog.preparation: Usually done in the same sitting as the standard hearing test. Avoid loud noise exposure for 16 hours beforehand if you can.

test_catalog.name: Speech Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Speech audiometry is a behavioural hearing test that measures a person’s ability to detect, recognise, and understand speech using standardised speech materials. It helps assess functional hearing and complements pure-tone audiometry. (Age range: 5 years and above.)
test_catalog.preparation: No preparation needed. The test is available in Tamil, English and Hindi — tell the audiologist which language you are most comfortable with.

test_catalog.name: Tympanometry
test_catalog.description: Tympanometry is an objective test of middle ear function that measures the mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane and middle ear system as air pressure in the external ear canal is varied. It is part of immittance audiometry. (Age range: applicable for all ages.)
test_catalog.preparation: Do not put oil, drops or cotton in the ear on the day of the test unless a doctor has told you to.

test_catalog.name: Acoustic Reflex Testing
test_catalog.description: Measures an automatic muscle response in the middle ear to loud sound. It helps locate where in the hearing pathway a problem lies. You will hear some loud but brief sounds.
test_catalog.preparation: Usually performed together with tympanometry. Tell the audiologist if loud sounds are painful for you.

test_catalog.name: Ear Examination (Otoscopy)
test_catalog.description: A visual look inside the ear canal and at the eardrum using a lighted instrument. It checks for wax, infection, fluid or a perforation before any hearing test is interpreted.
test_catalog.preparation: Do not attempt to clean the ear yourself, and do not use cotton buds. Wax is removed safely at the clinic if it is blocking the view.

test_catalog.name: Hearing Aid Electroacoustic Analysis
test_catalog.description: A bench test of the hearing aid itself in a small measuring chamber, to confirm it is still performing to specification. This checks the device, not the ear.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the hearing aid, its charger or spare batteries, and the earmould. Bring the second aid too if a pair is worn.

test_catalog.name: Play Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Conditioned Play Audiometry (CPA) is a behavioural hearing assessment technique in which a child is conditioned to perform a simple play activity (such as placing a block in a bucket or stacking rings) whenever an auditory stimulus is heard, allowing hearing thresholds to be obtained.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the child rested and fed. You can practise at home by playing a 'listen and drop the block' game with a hand clap so the idea is familiar. More than one visit is sometimes needed, which is normal at this age.

test_catalog.name: Aided Audiometry
test_catalog.description: Measures how well sound is heard while the hearing aid or implant is being worn. It shows what the device is actually delivering, in contrast to the unaided hearing test.
test_catalog.preparation: Wear or bring the device, fully charged, with the current earmould. Bring the device programming card or booklet if you have one.

test_catalog.name: Hearing Aid Evaluation
test_catalog.description: A consultation to decide whether a hearing aid would help, and if so which type suits your hearing, your ear and your daily life. Different models are demonstrated so you can hear the difference before deciding.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring your hearing test report if it was done elsewhere. Bring a family member if you can — a second opinion on how the sound feels is genuinely useful. Think beforehand about the situations you most want to hear better in.

test_catalog.name: Earmould Impression and Fitting
test_catalog.description: A soft impression material is placed briefly in the ear to make a custom earpiece. A well-fitting mould stops whistling and keeps the aid comfortable. Children outgrow moulds and need new ones regularly.
test_catalog.preparation: The ear must be free of infection and discharge on the day. The impression feels full but not painful, and sets in a few minutes.

test_catalog.name: Real Ear Measurement
test_catalog.description: A fine soft tube is placed alongside the hearing aid to measure the sound actually reaching the eardrum, then the aid is adjusted to the prescribed target. This is what turns an aid from switched-on to properly fitted.
test_catalog.preparation: Wear or bring the hearing aid and earmould. The ear canal must be clear of wax, so this may be checked first.

test_catalog.name: Device Check and Reprogramming
test_catalog.description: A service visit for a hearing aid or implant processor: the device is cleaned and tested, and the settings are adjusted if sound quality or comfort has changed.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the device, charger or batteries, earmould and any accessories. Note down beforehand when the problem happens — which situations, which ear, and whether it is constant or intermittent.

test_catalog.name: Dix-Hallpike Positional Test
test_catalog.description: A short bedside manoeuvre in which you are guided quickly from sitting to lying with the head turned, to look for the most common cause of positional vertigo. It provokes brief spinning on purpose, which is the finding being looked for.
test_catalog.preparation: Eat only lightly beforehand, since the test can cause brief nausea. Tell the clinician about any neck or back problem so the position can be adapted. Bring someone with you.

test_catalog.name: Balance Function Assessment
test_catalog.description: A set of standing, walking and head-movement tasks measuring how steady you are and where the difficulty comes from. It guides balance rehabilitation exercises.
test_catalog.preparation: Wear comfortable clothing and flat, well-fitting shoes. Bring your walking stick or frame if you use one. A staff member stays beside you throughout.

test_catalog.name: Tinnitus Assessment
test_catalog.description: Characterises the pitch and loudness of the sound you hear and measures how much it is affecting sleep, concentration and mood. This establishes a baseline for treatment.
test_catalog.preparation: Avoid loud noise for 24 hours beforehand. You will be asked how the tinnitus affects daily life, so it helps to think about specific examples, and to note for a few days when it is worst.

test_catalog.name: Tinnitus Retraining and Counselling
test_catalog.description: A structured programme combining explanation of why tinnitus happens with sound therapy and coping strategies, delivered over several sessions. The aim is to reduce the distress and intrusiveness rather than promise silence.
test_catalog.preparation: This runs across multiple appointments, so come prepared to attend a series. Bringing a family member to the first session helps them understand the condition too.

test_catalog.name: Speech and Language Assessment
test_catalog.description: A speech-language pathologist evaluates how speech and language are developing or have changed — what is understood, what is expressed, and how clearly. It produces a therapy plan with specific goals.
test_catalog.preparation: For a child, bring the immunisation and developmental record, any school report, and a list of the words or signs they currently use. Bring a favourite book or toy. For an adult, bring previous medical or discharge summaries.

test_catalog.name: Language Comprehension Assessment
test_catalog.description: Focuses specifically on understanding rather than speaking: following instructions, identifying objects, and grasping grammar. A child who understands well but speaks little has a different profile from one who understands little.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the child alert and fed. Note down at home which instructions they follow without gestures — that observation is valuable clinical information.

test_catalog.name: Articulation Assessment
test_catalog.description: Examines which speech sounds are produced correctly and which are substituted or omitted, and how understandable speech is to a stranger. It identifies exactly which sounds therapy should target.
test_catalog.preparation: Naming pictures aloud is involved, so a child who is comfortable talking to new people will give the best sample. Note any words family members consistently cannot understand.

test_catalog.name: Fluency (Stammering) Assessment
test_catalog.description: Measures the pattern and frequency of stammering across different speaking situations, and how much it is affecting confidence and participation. Both aspects shape the therapy plan.
test_catalog.preparation: If possible bring a short phone video of natural speech at home, since stammering often reduces in the clinic and the recording gives a truer picture. Note the situations that are hardest.

test_catalog.name: Voice Assessment
test_catalog.description: Evaluates voice quality, pitch, loudness and endurance, and how the voice is being produced. It identifies habits that strain the voice and can be changed.
test_catalog.preparation: Avoid shouting, whispering and throat-clearing for 24 hours, and avoid caffeine on the morning of the test. Do not skip a scheduled ENT examination of the vocal cords — voice therapy should not begin before the cords have been seen.

test_catalog.name: Motor Speech Examination
test_catalog.description: Assesses the strength, speed and coordination of the muscles used for speech — lips, tongue, palate and breath support. It distinguishes a muscle-control problem from a language problem, which need different therapy.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring any neurology reports, brain imaging results and your current medication list. Bring a family member who can describe how speech has changed over time.

test_catalog.name: Swallowing Assessment
test_catalog.description: Examines the safety of swallowing across different food and liquid textures, to identify whether anything is entering the airway. It leads to specific advice on textures and posture, and sometimes to further imaging.
test_catalog.preparation: Do not eat or drink for two hours beforehand unless told otherwise. Bring your usual thickener if you use one, and a list of foods that cause coughing. Tell the clinician about any recent chest infection or weight loss before starting.

test_catalog.name: ENT Specialist Referral
test_catalog.description: A medical examination by an ear, nose and throat doctor. Some findings need medical or surgical treatment that an audiologist cannot provide, and some need to be seen urgently.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring all hearing test reports, your current medicines, and any previous ear surgery or discharge records. If this referral was marked urgent, attend as soon as possible — in sudden hearing loss, treatment started within days works considerably better than treatment started later.

test_catalog.name: Laryngoscopy (ENT Examination of the Vocal Cords)
test_catalog.description: An ENT doctor looks directly at the vocal cords using a thin flexible scope passed through the nose, or a mirror. Any hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs the cords examined.
test_catalog.preparation: Eat only lightly beforehand. A numbing spray is used and the examination takes only a few minutes. Bring your voice assessment report if one has been done.

test_catalog.name: Developmental Paediatric Referral
test_catalog.description: An assessment by a developmental paediatrician covering all areas of a child's development, not hearing alone. It is arranged when the picture is broader than communication, or when skills have been lost.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the immunisation card, birth records, growth chart and any earlier assessments. Write down when you first noticed the concern and what changed — a clear timeline is the most useful thing you can bring.

test_catalog.name: Genetic Counselling Referral
test_catalog.description: A discussion with a genetics specialist about whether a hearing difference runs in the family and what that means for the child and for future pregnancies. It is information and support, not a test you must accept.
test_catalog.preparation: Ask relatives beforehand about hearing loss on both sides of the family, including at what age it started. Bring that family history and any consanguinity information, as it changes what the counsellor can tell you.

test_catalog.name: Early Intervention Programme Enrolment
test_catalog.description: Enrolment in the department's structured early intervention programme, combining regular therapy with parent training. For hearing and communication difficulties in young children, starting early makes a substantial difference to long-term outcome.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring all previous assessment reports and be ready to discuss which days you can attend regularly — consistent attendance matters more than intensity. Ask about travel support and fee concessions, which are available.

test_catalog.name: Auditory Verbal Therapy Review
test_catalog.description: A review of progress in listening and spoken language for a child using a hearing aid or implant. Goals are updated and the parent is coached in techniques to use at home.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring the device working and charged, the therapy diary if you keep one, and examples of new words or sounds noticed since the last visit.

test_catalog.name: Parent Counselling and Guidance
test_catalog.description: A dedicated session for parents to understand the diagnosis, ask questions without time pressure, and learn what to do at home. Consistent device use and daily communication practice depend far more on the family than on clinic visits.
test_catalog.preparation: Both parents or carers should attend if possible. Write your questions down beforehand — they are easy to forget in the room. There is no such thing as a question that is too basic here.

test_catalog.name: Scheduled Follow-up Hearing Review
test_catalog.description: A planned repeat review to confirm that hearing, speech or device performance remains stable. Some conditions change slowly and are only detected by comparing results over time.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring your previous reports so results can be compared directly. Attend even if nothing seems to have changed — that comparison is the purpose of the visit. Contact the department earlier if anything worsens in the meantime.

test_catalog.name: Western Aphasia Battery (WAB)
test_catalog.description: Evaluates spontaneous speech, comprehension, repetition and naming. It is used mainly when language has changed after a stroke or brain injury, and gives a structured picture of which language skills need support.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring any neurology or stroke discharge summaries, recent brain imaging reports, and a family member who can describe how talking and understanding have changed. Wear glasses or hearing aids if you use them.

test_catalog.name: Speech-Language Evaluation
test_catalog.description: A speech-language evaluation reviews how you understand and use language, how clearly you speak, and which skills would benefit from therapy. It is the usual first assessment for adult speech and language concerns.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring previous medical or discharge summaries, glasses or hearing aids if you use them, and a family member who can describe day-to-day communication.

test_catalog.name: Fluency Assessment
test_catalog.description: Looks at how smoothly speech flows, including repetitions, blocks and avoidance, and how much this is affecting confidence and daily speaking situations.
test_catalog.preparation: If possible bring a short recording of natural speech at home. Note the situations that feel hardest, such as phone calls or speaking in a group.

test_catalog.name: Speech Sound / Clarity Assessment
test_catalog.description: Checks which speech sounds are clear, which are slurred or imprecise, and how understandable speech is to others. It identifies which sounds need support.
test_catalog.preparation: Come ready to talk at a comfortable pace. Note words that others often cannot understand, and whether speech is worse when you are tired.

test_catalog.name: Voice Assessment
test_catalog.description: Reviews voice quality, strain, pitch, loudness and how the voice holds up through the day, so habits that tire the voice can be identified.
test_catalog.preparation: Avoid shouting, whispering and throat-clearing for 24 hours if you can. Bring any ENT reports about the vocal cords, and note when the voice is worst.

test_catalog.name: Linguistic Profile Test (LPT)
test_catalog.description: Profiles language across sounds, word forms, sentence structure, and meaning. It is used with adults and with older children so therapy can focus on the areas that need most support.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring glasses or hearing aids if you use them, and any previous speech or language reports. A family member who knows how communication is at home can add useful context at the start of the session.

test_catalog.name: Assessment of Language Development (ALD)
test_catalog.description: Checks how a child understands and uses language against age-expected milestones, so the clinician can see which language skills are on track and which need support.
test_catalog.preparation: Bring any previous speech or language reports and a parent or caregiver who knows how the child communicates at home and at school. Hearing aids or glasses should be worn if the child uses them.

test_catalog.name: Receptive-Expressive Emergent Language Scale (REELS)
test_catalog.description: Assesses early receptive and expressive language in infants and toddlers, looking at how the child understands others and how they begin to use sounds, gestures, and words.
test_catalog.preparation: A parent or caregiver who knows the child’s daily communication should attend. Bring a favourite toy if it helps the child settle. Hearing aids or glasses should be worn if the child uses them.

test_catalog.name: COMDEALL Developmental Checklist
test_catalog.description: Screens broader developmental and communication milestones. It is often used when Autism Spectrum concerns are suspected, alongside a speech and language review.
test_catalog.preparation: A parent or caregiver who knows the child’s play, social interaction, and daily routines should attend. Bring any previous developmental or paediatric reports if you have them.
